item.title: Topological Josephson trijunctions as a Majorana source and path
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 07 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79077-5

Manipulating Majorana bound states is a key requirement for topological quantum computation. Here, the authors propose a topological insulator Josephson trijunction in a magnetic field that enables the generation, transport, and fusion of Majorana bound states through static control of superconducting phases.
item.dc:title: Topological Josephson trijunctions as a Majorana source and path

item.title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates Pseudomonas aeruginosa surface colonization and virulence
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 07 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79432-6

Second messengers cAMP and c-di-GMP regulate surface behaviours and virulence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Here, the authors show how the bacteria switch between attachment and surface movement by coordinating the two signalling systems, allowing distinct bacterial populations to work together to colonise and damage human airway tissue.
item.dc:title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates Pseudomonas aeruginosa surface colonization and virulence

item.title: Selective depolymerization of poly(ethylene terephthalate) for economical closed-loop recycling of mixed textiles
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 07 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78713-4

Recovering polymerization-grade monomers from waste textiles remains challenging. Here the authors report that the depolymerization of PET from thermally treated mixed textiles via methanolysis can be achieved in a rapid yet highly selective manner under mild conditions.

item.title: Nanofluid wetting of Cu enables thin lithium negative electrodes for high-energy and long-cycling lithium metal batteries
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 07 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79376-x

Lithium metal batteries face trade-offs between energy density and cycling life owing to lithium processability and plating challenges. Here, authors develop a nanofluid-wetting method to fabricate thin Li foils down to 800 nm, which enables anode-lean pouch cells with 498 Wh kg–1 / 1,142 Wh L–1 and stable cycling over 250 cycles.
item.dc:title: Nanofluid wetting of Cu enables thin lithium negative electrodes for high-energy and long-cycling lithium metal batteries

item.title: Insular motor and error encoding supports self-correcting intracranial brain-computer interface
item.description:
Paul Weger, Sophia Gimple, Maarten C. Ottenhoff, Maxime Verwoert, Lauren Ostrowski, Albert Colon, Louis Wagner, Johannes P. van Dijk, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78804-2
Abstract Error recognition is fundamental to adaptive behavior, enabling rapid compensatory action when outcomes deviate from expectations. Central to this function are neural circuits for performance monitoring, encoding cognitive signals that could support more reliable neural interfaces. Here, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) in epilepsy patients to enable a motor brain-computer interface (BCI) while sampling error-related activity across a distributed network. Our work reveals high-frequency population dynamics emerging in the anterior insula and propagating to the prefrontal cortex as the interface fails to follow the user’s intention. We identify spatially organized insular responses to error processing and movement feedback, highlighting it as a heterogeneous hub linking action and outcome. Frontoinsular recording sites were found to preferentially encode error-related activity, while centroparietal responses were intermixed with compensatory motor signals, making the former a compelling target for real-time error correction. Together, our findings demonstrate a human intracranial BCI harnessing insular brain activity, integrating cognitive processes directly into device control.

item.title: Ultra-high precision speckle spectrometer enabling radio-frequency scale resolution of atomic spectra
item.description:
Gabriel Britto Monteiro, Christopher Perrella, Sarah K. Scholten, Morgan Facchin, Andre N. Luiten, Graham D. Bruce, Kishan Dholakia
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78325-y
Abstract Laser speckle, the granular intensity pattern arising from random optical interference, provides a high-dimensional encoding of spectral information that can be exploited for precision metrology. Speckle-based spectrometers have advanced rapidly owing to their compact footprint, mechanical robustness and alignment agnostic nature, yet their spectral resolution has remained limited to the picometre scale. In this work, we break this limit by employing an integrating sphere as a multiply scattering cavity with access to a high range of path lengths to enhance spectral sensitivity. At 780 nm, the resulting device achieves a resolution of 6 fm, corresponding to a resolving power of 1.3 × 10 8 , representing an approximately 80-fold improvement over previous implementations. This ultra-high resolution enables clear discrimination of laser sidebands generated by an electro-optical modulator, with extracted sideband powers agreeing with expected values to within 1%. It further permits a direct speckle-based measurement of the hyperfine structure of the D 2 transition in 85 Rb, with transmission spectra differing by no more than 3.7% from independent wavemeter-referenced measurements. These results establish speckle as a platform for ultra-high precision spectroscopy, radio-frequency spectrometry, and microwave photonics.

item.title: Non-canonical FOXO1 signaling governs epithelial barrier integrity through spatial regulation of the E-cadherin–β-catenin complex
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78640-4

Bacterial challenge rapidly weakens epithelial barriers through a non-canonical, FOXO1–β-catenin–E-cadherin axis that disrupts adherens junctions and redistributes E-cadherin independently of transcription or proteolysis.

item.title: Resolving phonons in superconductor Bi<sub>2</sub>Sr<sub>2</sub>CaCu<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8+δ</sub> at sub-unit-cell resolution
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77617-7

The role of phonons in cuprate superconductivity remains debated, partly because their layered structures host complex lattice dynamics. Here, sub-unit-cell spectroscopy resolves layer-localized phonons in Bi-2212 and reveals a spatial correlation between superstructure-driven phonon frequency modulations and superconducting gap variations.
